/projects/era-centennial-convention.title: ERA Centennial Convention - Jason Zhang
/projects/era-centennial-convention.description: Jason Zhang is a visual designer and Computer Science student at the University of Michigan Ann Arbor.
p: Branding

Visual Design for the ERA Centennial Convention, a joint effort between the Young Feminist Party, Colombia Law School, ERA Coalition, National Organization of Women, and more in Seneca Falls, NY celebrating the Equal Rights Amendment's 100th anniversary.

The ERA Centennial Convention ran July 21-22, 2023, in Seneca Falls, marking 100 years since Alice Paul first introduced the Equal Rights Amendment. Organized by Generation Ratify, Equal Rights Action, and Columbia Law School’s ERA Project, it brought together activists, scholars, and advocates to look back on a century of organizing and figure out what full constitutional recognition of the ERA actually takes from here. We held it in the First Presbyterian Church of Seneca Falls, the same building where Paul unveiled the ERA in 1923, which made the history hard to ignore even before anyone spoke.

As the visual and brand designer, I owned everything attendees would actually see: social graphics, printed programs, banners, workshop materials. The identity needed to hold two things at once, the weight of a hundred years of organizing and the sense that attendees were part of what came next, not just there to observe it.

I built the design around circles, a nod to the ripple effect of a century of organizing, and to the original ‘ERA YES’ campaign button. Archival photos of suffrage parades and ERA demonstrations sit in the backgrounds of a lot of the materials, and the green-and-white palette comes straight from the suffragist movement, so the visual line from 1923 to 2023 is pretty literal. Type stayed bold enough to read from across a room but plain enough to hold up on a printed handout.

The promo materials for the Reimagining Gender Justice workshop series, which ran in the weeks before the convention, had to represent a genuinely wide coalition: queer activists, women of color, constitutional scholars, people working on gender justice globally. I wanted someone who’d been organizing for decades and someone showing up for the first time to look at the same poster and both feel like it was made for them.

Accessibility mattered as much as aesthetics here. Signage needed high contrast to actually help people navigate the church and surrounding venues, and the printed schedules had to lay out two days of programming clearly enough that nobody missed a session hunting for information. The large banners did double duty as wayfinding and as a way to make the space feel unified rather than like a church with some posters taped up.

/projects/one-finance-app-redesign.title: ONE Finance App Redesign - Jason Zhang
/projects/one-finance-app-redesign.description: Jason Zhang is a visual designer and Computer Science student at the University of Michigan Ann Arbor.
p: UI/UX
UI/UX Concept Design for ONE Finance, a neobank now owned by Walmart.

I’m actually a ONE Finance customer, and this redesign started from my own frustration with the app. Pockets, their system for splitting money into categories like Utilities or Savings Goals, is a genuinely good idea, but the interface buried it under extra taps to get to virtual cards, transaction history, or spending insights.

I mapped out the existing user journey first, marked where I kept getting stuck, and sketched new flows for the actions that mattered most: creating a virtual card for a specific pocket, linking a merchant category to a spending rule. Both should have taken a few taps, not a small investigation.

Each Pocket became its own card showing balance, recent activity, and the controls you’d actually want, auto-save toggles, spend limits, right there instead of another screen deep. I added subtle shadows and contextual highlights to give the interface some depth without it turning busy.

I built the whole system to work in both light and dark mode from the start rather than bolting dark mode on afterward. Light mode stays warm and legible; dark mode leans into higher contrast for checking your balance at night without getting blasted by a white screen.

Virtual card management got a full rework too. Generating a card, labeling it, setting a usage limit or expiration, all of that now lives in one view instead of being scattered across the fragmented flow the original app had.
This one was a passion project more than a client engagement, a chance to fix the specific things that annoyed me as an actual user rather than guess at what a hypothetical one might want.

/projects/thoyen-redesign.title: THOYEN App Redesign  - Jason Zhang
/projects/thoyen-redesign.description: Jason Zhang is a visual designer and Computer Science student at the University of Michigan Ann Arbor.
p: UI/UX
UI/UX Design for THOYEN, a platform-based freelance service app connecting customers to college students looking to earn extra income.

THOYEN brought me on in early 2021 to redesign their app, think TaskRabbit but built for college campuses. Students pick up odd jobs, cleaning, moving help, tutoring, for extra cash, and an automatic matching system assigns tasks based on their profile, which they can accept or turn down.

My job was to build one design system that worked across mobile and web without feeling like two different products. Students on THOYEN are busy and checking the app between classes, so I optimized for speed and clarity over anything flashy.

I started with a full audit of the existing UI and talked to stakeholders to find the actual pain points: profile customization, payment processing, and task tracking kept coming up. The trickiest part was designing for two very different users, students doing tasks and customers hiring them, without building two separate apps that happened to share a name.

The redesigned dashboard puts earnings, ratings, and available tasks front and center, with a bottom nav bar for the stuff people check constantly: active tasks, schedule, profile. I added small feedback animations for moments like accepting a task or completing a transaction, mostly so the app didn’t feel like it was ignoring you when you tapped something important.

Payments got the biggest overhaul. Linking a card or bank account used to be confusing, so I simplified that flow while keeping it clear what was actually happening with someone’s financial info. I also went back through everything for basic accessibility, text scaling and tap target sizes especially, since a lot of this app gets used one-handed while walking to class.
For rewards and discounts, I designed an offers section built around cards that surface the deal terms without shouting over the rest of the app.

The design system I built is meant to scale as THOYEN adds features, not get rebuilt every time the app grows. What shipped is a more usable version of the same idea: a straightforward way for students to find paid work on their own campus.

/projects/roam.title: ROAM - Jason Zhang
/projects/roam.description: Jason Zhang is a visual designer and Computer Science student at the University of Michigan Ann Arbor.
p: Product
UI/UX Design & Brand Identity for ROAM, a new marketplace for the metaverse putting creators first. ROAM is a place for artists to share, sell, and protect their 3D assets and models.
ROAM is a marketplace built specifically for 3D asset creators working in VR and the metaverse, a place to upload, showcase, and sell work with real protection against people just ripping it off.

Right now, most 3D creators are stuck selling through generalist platforms like Gumroad or just sending files over Discord, neither built for 3D work or for protecting it. ROAM is 3D-only, with DRM and watermarking built specifically for that file type, so creators keep control of their work and buyers can trust what they’re paying for is the real thing.

I owned brand strategy, visual identity, and the web design end to end, making sure the way the platform looked matched what it was actually trying to do: give creators a secure place to sell work and get paid for it.

The brand started with the ‘://’ from a URL, the piece of the internet’s own syntax that nobody thinks about, reworked as a symbol of connection for a web3 audience. From there I kept the aesthetic sleek and technical, closer to what a digital artist or developer would actually want to look at than a typical marketplace.

Uploading and browsing were the two flows I cared about most. Search and filtering are tuned to how 3D assets actually get described, polycount, file format, rigging, not generic tags, and creator profiles double as portfolios so reputation builds over time instead of resetting with every listing.

/projects/stately-credit.title: Stately Credit - Jason Zhang
/projects/stately-credit.description: Jason Zhang is a visual designer and Computer Science student at the University of Michigan Ann Arbor.
p: UI/UX
UI/UX Design for Stately Credit, an up-and-coming startup in the financial space. Created both a web and mobile optimized experience for consumer banking and borrowing.

Stately Credit is a fintech startup building an all-in-one banking product: personal banking, savings, budgeting, payday loans, and financial education all in one place. My job was to design a system that held together across mobile and web without just stretching one layout to fit the other, since the two platforms get used completely differently.

The dashboard had to do two things that usually fight each other: show someone their whole financial picture at a glance, and still let them dig into specifics. Pockets, Stately’s feature for splitting an account into sub-categories for specific goals or expenses, became the centerpiece. I built a visual way to move money between Pockets and track progress toward each one, plus default deposit rules so a chunk of every paycheck routes into savings automatically instead of requiring someone to remember to do it.

Consistency across devices meant building an actual design system: shared typography, iconography, and components rather than one-off screens. I paid particular attention to users who aren’t financially fluent, since a lot of fintech UI assumes everyone already understands APRs and compounding, and Stately’s audience often doesn’t.

I worked closely with product and engineering to get the prototypes right, and usability testing kept surfacing real gaps between what I assumed users understood and what they actually did. That feedback loop is what pushed the interface toward simpler explanations rather than more polished ones.
The version that shipped gives users a clearer read on where their money is and an easier way to move it where it needs to go, which was the actual goal from the start.

/projects/ballotwise.title: BallotWise - Jason Zhang
/projects/ballotwise.description: Jason Zhang is a visual designer and Computer Science student at the University of Michigan Ann Arbor.
p: Product

Visual Design & Brand Identity for BallotWise, a new nonpartisan tool aimed at helping undecided and non-politically engaged voters learn more about the candidates on their ballot and their stance on key issues, empowering them to make informed decisions before Election Day.
A project created by students from:
Featured in:

BallotWise shows undecided voters a preview of their actual ballot, then breaks down each candidate’s real, tangible actions in Congress instead of just their talking points: plain-English summaries of real bills paired with how they actually voted. We picked the bills using the ten issues the New York Times/Siena poll found voters cared about most in the 2024 cycle.

That’s the whole point: showing a candidate’s actions, not just their promises. We built it with young and lower-income voters in swing states in mind, since they’re the ones least likely to have time to dig through voting records themselves, so they can walk into the booth with an actual plan.
You enter your zip code, no account needed, and we pull your specific races and candidates from the Google Civics API.

You get a preview of your actual ballot and can browse each candidate to see how they voted on real congressional bills tied to the biggest issues of the 2024 cycle. Each bill gets a nonpartisan summary, drafted by GPT-4o and checked by a policy expert, of what it actually would have done.
You pick who you’re voting for, and BallotWise builds you a personalized voting guide to bring into the booth.
For the visual identity, I was chasing a specific balance: something trustworthy enough for a civic tool but still approachable, not another sterile government-adjacent website.

Color was the first real decision. I built a gradient that moves from red to blue and meets in a neutral middle, a literal picture of BallotWise not leaning either direction. Everything sits on plain white, which keeps the palette from feeling gimmicky and matches the transparency the platform is actually built around.

For the logo and supporting materials, I went with Geller, a serif that reads the way newspapers and government documents read: established, credible, a little formal. I paired it with Area, a plainer sans-serif, for everything else, so the brand didn’t feel stuck in the past alongside all that gravitas.

The one place I let myself get playful was the W in the wordmark, built from two hand-drawn checkmarks. It’s a small nod to voting, and the slightly imperfect linework keeps the whole thing from reading as another sterile civic-tech product. Voting is personal; the logo should look like it knows that.

This took a few rounds to land. My first pass leaned hard on modern sans-serif type, and it read as clinical instead of empowering, so I went back to the serif to anchor things in trust. The checkmark W came later, after I realized the logo needed more personality and a symbol people would recognize instantly without being too on the nose.

Put together, the serif type, the hand-drawn checkmark, and the neutral color scheme all point at the same thing: BallotWise is here to inform, not to sway anyone. That was the brief from day one, and I wanted the brand to make the case before a user ever reads a word of copy.

/projects/young-feminist-party.title: Young Feminist Party - Jason Zhang
/projects/young-feminist-party.description: Jason Zhang is a visual designer and Computer Science student at the University of Michigan Ann Arbor.
p: Branding

Visual Design & Brand Identity for the Young Feminist Party, a nationwide, youth-led social movement advocating for gender equality. Created the brand from the ground up for the web, social, and physical print.

As YFP’s visual designer, I led our full rebrand: from Generation Ratify, a group built around one goal, ratifying the ERA, into Young Feminist Party, a national youth movement covering reproductive rights, pay equity, and gender justice more broadly. That wasn’t a coat of paint, it reflected an actual shift in what we stood for. With over 10,000 members and 30-plus chapters across the country by that point, the brand needed to hold a national network together while still leaving room for individual chapters to make it their own.
Featured in:

Since the rebrand, our Instagram has passed 12,000 followers and site traffic is up over 300%. We’ve also built partnerships with groups like Gen-Z for Change, FEMINIST, Columbia Law School, Women’s March, and the National Organization for Women. Together, our network now reaches more than 7 million young people across the country. YFP’s own accounts pull over 2 million views a month. The modular system means local chapters can put together their own materials and still look unmistakably like YFP, and we’ve launched more than 15 new chapters in the past year alone.

I built the brand around one image: an umbrella. The ERA is sometimes called an umbrella amendment because it protects such a wide range of issues, workplace equality, education access, reproductive justice, and the icon is a literal version of that idea. The logo itself is built to be modular: the O has a cutout that individual chapters and campaigns can customize, so a local chapter’s materials still read as YFP without looking identical to every other chapter’s.

The palette runs on Radiant Purple, ERA Green, and Vibrant Blue, with gradients that keep things feeling active rather than static. Headers are bold and declarative; body text stays plain and legible, since a lot of this brand lives on a phone screen. For bigger initiatives, like our voter education and reproductive rights campaigns, I built sub-brands with their own colors and taglines that still trace back to the core system, so a major campaign can stand on its own without splitting off from YFP entirely.
The website needed the same overhaul. I rebuilt it around the new identity and cut down how many clicks it took to find a chapter, an event, or a campaign, since the old site buried all three.

I also run YFP’s social accounts day to day, which means the brand gets tested constantly instead of just living in a style guide. Most of what I make is graphics and short videos for Instagram and Twitter: member spotlights, breakdowns of what a new bill actually does, calls to action for upcoming events.

/projects/empower.title: EMPOWER Michigan - Jason Zhang
/projects/empower.description: Jason Zhang is a visual designer and Computer Science student at the University of Michigan Ann Arbor.
p: Branding

Brand Identity for Empower Michigan's bold and student-driven campaign for the University of Michigan's Central Student Government. Empower Michigan is a diverse, apolitical party founded to advance the interests of all students at the University of Michigan

Empower Michigan brought me on to design their brand for a Central Student Government race at the University of Michigan. I needed one visual identity that could hold up across flyers, Instagram posts, and full-screen digital slides, while still reading as one campaign no matter where you ran into it.

Their platform centered on accessibility, affordability, and student wellness, and I wanted the design to feel like it came from the same place: clear, confident, and built around community rather than any one candidate.

The centerpiece of the brand is a custom M built entirely out of bold yellow dots, my twist on the University of Michigan’s block M. Every dot stands for something separate: a distinct idea, community, or lived experience that only becomes the full letter once it’s part of the group.

That’s the whole idea behind Empower Michigan too: real change on campus happens when different students, commuters, grad students, marginalized groups, everyone with a stake, show up and work together. The dotted M is just that idea rendered as a logo.
Unity through collective action, strength through difference, not despite it.

For type, I went heavy and confident, matching how assertive Empower’s platform was on things like reproductive care access and campus safety at night. I kept Michigan’s maize and blue, since ditching official school colors felt like a nonstarter, but pushed the contrast harder than you’d see in a typical university branding guide.

I built the system to hold up anywhere: campaign slides, business cards, event signage, Instagram graphics. Wherever a student ran into Empower’s brand, on a table in the Union or in their feed, it needed to read as the same campaign.

/projects/feminist-generation.title: Feminist Generation - Jason Zhang
/projects/feminist-generation.description: Jason Zhang is a visual designer and Computer Science student at the University of Michigan Ann Arbor.
p: Branding

I led the complete rebrand of Feminist Generation, a new organization formed from the merger of Young Feminist Party and Feminist Front. Drawing on riot grrrl punk and DIY protest culture, I built a bold, flexible identity system that unified grassroots energy with the polish needed for national campaigns.

When Young Feminist Party and Feminist Front merged into a new, unified organization, there was both excitement and pressure to create an identity that reflected not just a name change but an entirely new era of feminist organizing. I had been working with Young Feminist Party already, so when the merger came together, I was tasked with leading the design of a complete rebrand. It wasn’t simply about designing a new logo—it was about translating our collective vibe, energy, and values into a brand system that felt alive, powerful, and unmistakably our own.

From the very first conversations, there was a clear sense of what the identity needed to feel like. We all agreed that it had to be fresh and unapologetically punk, pulling directly from the riot grrrl feminist movement of the 70s and its legacy of zines, posters, and DIY culture. We wanted the brand to have a scrapbook energy, something that carried the marks of imperfection and human touch, while still being clean and legible enough to work across digital platforms and professional communications. The vibe we were chasing was spunky and powerful, rebellious but intentional, grassroots while still polished enough to be taken seriously by national partners and funders.

That spirit shaped every decision in the design process. Typography became one of the first elements where the riot grrrl energy came through. I built the system around Decalotype, a bold, geometric sans-serif that can be pushed to extremes for big, declarative headlines. Its heavy weight gave us the power and presence we needed for protest-style graphics. Rather than relying on one typeface alone, I layered in Inter as a versatile, highly legible workhorse font for body copy and flexible layouts. The contrast between Decalotype’s punch and Inter’s neutrality gave us range. To keep that raw, zine-inspired edge, I introduced JetBrains Mono into the system. Its monospaced, typewriter feel evoked the handmade, the photocopied, the “scrapbooked together” ethos we wanted. Together, these three typefaces created a typographic voice that could be loud and in-your-face one moment and quietly functional the next.

Color followed a similar path of balancing chaos and clarity. As a team, we kept coming back to neon brights and high-contrast tones—shades that felt electric, rebellious, and in-your-face. Acid lime, chrome blue, and electric violet became our “riot colors,” the ones that popped most aggressively in digital and print. To ground them, I built the palette out with deep violet, forest green, and a true charcoal black. This way, we could dial the system up to full anarchic brightness when we wanted energy, or mute it down to something steadier when we needed seriousness. The green—eventually named FG Neon—emerged as our signature, tying together the visuals with a color that was both accessible and striking. The palette itself ended up carrying the contradiction we wanted: youthful and playful, but grounded in history and purpose.

The logo was one of the most iterative parts of the process. Early sketches played with stencil textures, geometric forms, and bold typographic treatments. I explored versions that leaned heavily on type, versions with boxed-in protest-stamp aesthetics, and variations that brought the initials “FG” into focus. Each draft was an attempt to capture the duality of the brand: punk rawness on one hand, organizational clarity on the other.

Through testing these directions with the team, one motif kept rising to the surface: the star. Rough, hand-drawn, and a little imperfect, the star carried both the grassroots energy of screen printing and hand drawn signs and the optimism of spotlighting youth voices. Once paired with the type system, the star achieved the balance we were looking for—it felt like something you could stencil on a wall or scrawl on a sign, but it also had the authority to stand as a national brand mark. Those early explorations were essential; by pushing wide in every direction, we could distill down to the logo that carried the most authenticity.

Once the foundational elements were in place, I began experimenting with how type, imagery, and texture could come together. Halftone effects became essential, not just for their punk aesthetic but because they connected today’s activism to a long legacy of protest print culture. Black-and-white photographs of marches and rallies, processed into gritty halftones, became the backdrop for bold type. Rough brush strokes and jagged star patterns created motion and urgency. Big, all-caps headlines stacked vertically gave the work a cadence that felt like a chant. The designs didn’t just look like posters; they sounded like protest.

What made this process most powerful was how collaborative it was. The rebrand wasn’t me designing in a vacuum—it was me absorbing the energy of our team, who were organizers first and foremost. Their language, their slogans, and their sense of urgency shaped every visual decision. When they said something needed to feel louder, I leaned harder into the bold weights. When they wanted something to feel grassroots, I layered in halftone photos and textures that looked rough around the edges. When they needed materials to be flexible for chapters across the country, I designed modular templates that could handle local event details without losing brand consistency.

In the end, the Feminist Generation rebrand captured something rare: a brand identity that feels as if it was built on the streets, even when it’s polished enough for boardrooms. It brought together the DIY power of the riot grrrl movement with the needs of a national organization, creating a look that was both rebellious and strategic. Most importantly, it gave young feminists across the country a visual language that reflected their own energy—a brand that looked like the movement they were already building, now unified under one name.
‹ Harvest

/projects/harvest.title: Harvest - Jason Zhang
/projects/harvest.description: Jason Zhang is a visual designer and Computer Science student at the University of Michigan Ann Arbor.
p: Hackathon
A grocery-app-style platform that unifies Southeast Michigan's food pantries into one real-time, dignity-first shopping experience — built with four teammates in a single day.

I built Harvest over one day with four teammates — Serena Flaxenburg, Natalie Mark, Chloe Tjakra, and Ashley Yeung — for the Google × CSG × T4SG Hackathon for Social Good, a competition focused on Digital Public Infrastructure: the open data platforms, public APIs, civic dashboards, and benefit-distribution tools that make public services more efficient and accessible. Teams picked from five urban problem tracks. We built at the intersection of Government Services & Access and Resource Allocation & Sustainability, with one constraint shaping everything: ship a working, demoable MVP by the end of the day.

Washtenaw County's food insecurity rate has climbed to 14%, touching roughly 51,000 residents. That's not because the food isn't there — local food banks distribute over 107 million pounds of it annually through 700-plus partner agencies. Nationally, the EPA estimates food banks discard more than a billion pounds of food a year to spoilage, even as demand outpaces what reaches people. The gap sits in coordination, not supply. Most pantries run on brutally narrow hours, some as little as sixty minutes a week. Fewer than half of food-insecure residents qualify for SNAP. And transportation insecurity now affects more Americans, 19%, than food insecurity itself, which means even a well-stocked pantry two miles away might as well not exist for someone without a car.
We treated this as a coordination failure rather than a supply shortage. The food and the need both exist. What's missing is the layer that connects them in real time.

Harvest reframes food assistance as an ordinary consumer errand instead of a charity transaction. Rather than asking someone to memorize which pantry is open when, and hope the thing they need hasn't already been claimed, Harvest shows food access the way a grocery delivery app shows groceries: browse, add to cart, pick up or get it delivered.

Critically, the product sits on top of infrastructure that already exists rather than replacing it. Pantries keep using their own inventory tools — Link2Feed, ConnectFood, whatever they've already got — and Harvest acts as the aggregation layer that pulls that data together and makes it visible to the people who need it.

The consumer side had to feel indistinguishable from any mainstream delivery app, because that familiarity is the whole point. Users browse real-time inventory from nearby pantries organized into the categories you'd expect — produce, dairy, bread & grains, protein, canned goods, frozen, snacks, beverages — with dietary filters for gluten-free, dairy-free, nut-free, egg-free, fish-free, and vegan.

On top of that, an AI recipe feature reads whatever's actually in stock nearby and suggests nutrient-dense, healthy meals built from it, so people can plan around what's available instead of guessing or making a wasted trip.

Requesting items works through a standard cart flow, with a choice between pickup or delivery at checkout. We were deliberate about what the interface never shows: no countdown timers, no "expiring soon" badges, no scarcity language anywhere in the consumer-facing UI. That was non-negotiable for us as a team. Urgency logic runs entirely in the backend — accessing food assistance should never feel different from any other errand.

Each item's detail page pulls real nutrition and ingredient data, sourced automatically through the barcode pipeline on the pantry side, so a user browsing a can of tuna or a case of energy drinks sees the same nutrition facts and ingredient list they'd get scanning it themselves at a store. Transparency here mattered as much as speed.

We built dedicated accessibility controls rather than assuming default styling would work for everyone: large text, high contrast, reduced motion for vestibular disorders, and enhanced focus indicators for keyboard navigation, all saved automatically and layered on top of whatever system-level settings a person already has enabled.

Behind the consumer app, Harvest is built as a data aggregation layer that pulls from the tools pantries already run: inventory platforms like Link2Feed and ConnectFood, volunteer coordination through Food Rescue Hero, logistics and routing through BringFood. Consolidating those into one operational picture is what lets a pantry get smarter about what its community actually needs, instead of just reacting to whatever's in front of them.

None of the consumer experience works without pantry staff actually logging what they have, so the staff dashboard had to be fast enough to survive real operating conditions. The overview screen gives staff total inventory count, pending orders awaiting confirmation, and anything expiring within 48 hours, all in one glance.
The inventory table underneath lets staff track item, category, quantity, and expiration date, with quick edit and delete actions per row.

The feature I'm proudest of is the barcode scanner. Staff point a camera at a product barcode, and the system pulls product images and nutrition data automatically from the OpenFoodFacts API — what used to be manual data entry collapses into a few seconds. It's a small piece of the build, but it's the difference between a tool pantry staff will actually use under time pressure and one they'll quietly abandon after week one.

On the order side, staff see incoming requests with the items involved and can mark them ready for pickup with one tap. Behind the scenes, expiration-aware logic quietly prioritizes soon-to-expire items in both the consumer shopping feed and the recipe suggestions, and widens the delivery radius automatically if something isn't claimed in time — all invisible to the person browsing.

We didn't try to build a driver network in a day, and honestly we wouldn't want to even with more time. Harvest is architected to plug into delivery infrastructure that already has a track record, like DoorDash's Project DASH, which has run a validated food-pantry delivery pilot with Food Gatherers right here in Ann Arbor. For pantries running their own volunteer programs, the same modular approach lets Harvest hand off to tools like BringFood or Food Rescue Hero instead of competing with them.

The frontend is Next.js on Vercel. Inventory enrichment runs through the OpenFoodFacts API for barcode-based product lookup. Recipe suggestions come from an LLM reading live inventory data. All of it, front to back, shipped within the single-day hackathon window.

/projects/adlib.title: Adlib - Jason Zhang
/projects/adlib.description: Jason Zhang is a visual designer and Computer Science student at the University of Michigan Ann Arbor.
h4: Learning What Someone Actually Wants to Try
Turning a Notification into a Yes
Booking, Social Proof, and Coming Back
p: Hackathon

A concept app surfacing last-minute, discounted spots in local workshops, fitness classes, and events, turning unsold capacity into a low-stakes way to try something new tonight. Placed 2nd at Converge 2026, a 5-hour designathon organized by FLUX.

Converge 2026 is a 5-hour designathon organized by FLUX, and this year’s theme was Parallel Lives: how people can experiment with different identities, paths, and interests without much risk or commitment. The prompt pushed us to ask why so many alternate versions of a person’s life stay hypothetical: the hobby they never tried, the class they kept meaning to take, the version of themselves they’re curious about but never became. Time, money, and the fear of disrupting an existing routine get in the way every time.

I worked with three teammates: Felicia Wang, George Gu, and Eva Chong, under FLUX’s constraints: design from scratch, any assets, AI use allowed if disclosed, five hours from concept to a presentable pitch.

Our read on the brief was that a fantasy simulator would miss the point. Nobody needed a mood board for the life they’re not living, or another app to help them plan out their life—for us, we wanted to make it as easy as possible to actually do something new. So we set out to design something that made a real new experience feel low-stakes enough to say yes to on short notice.

The day broke into four blocks: an hour of research and ideation, ninety minutes of wireframing and structure, ninety minutes of high-fidelity design, and thirty minutes packaging everything into a pitch, with a lunch break wedged into the middle. Sixty minutes in, we landed on the mechanic that became Adlib: unsold inventory meets curious people.

Working with Felicia on UX and product design, we owned the middle two blocks, turning that raw mechanic into an actual flow. How does someone discover a nearby opening, decide it’s worth their evening, and book it, and what does that experience need to look and feel like so trying something new tonight reads as easy instead of intimidating? That flow became the backbone the rest of the deck, the business model and the pitch narrative, got built around.

The first screens I designed handle onboarding. Instead of a static list of categories, we opened with a blunt prompt, what do you want to try, and let people answer in their own words: pottery, DJing, boxing, whatever they’ve been putting off. From there, a short set-your-vibe step collects budget, distance, and time preference, so the feed that follows is already narrowed to what someone would actually say yes to. A lightweight profile with an aura-points system sits behind it, turning attendance into a small, visible track record rather than a one-off transaction.

Adlib works like a marketplace for spontaneity. Businesses list last-minute openings: two empty wheels at a pottery studio tonight, unfilled spots in a boxing class, unsold tickets an hour before a show, at a discount. Users see what’s available nearby, right now, and can book in a couple of taps.

We designed the discovery layer around a push notification and a single swipeable card, closer to a dating app than an events listing. A notification about last-minute spots opening up drops straight into the card: the venue, who else is already going, how many spots are left, with only two decisions to make, pass or join. Cutting the interaction down to one card and one choice was the whole point. Every extra tap was a chance for someone to talk themselves out of it.

Saying yes drops into an event detail page with a map, a host, and a join-the-crowd list showing who from your circle is already attending, the social proof that makes showing up to a stranger’s DJ workshop feel less like a risk. Booking happens with Apple Pay in the same screen. Underneath it all, an aura-points system rewards attendance and spend, unlocking profile customization, priority access to future drops, and cash back at higher tiers, a small loop meant to turn a one-time impulse booking into a habit.

The design goal underneath all of it was removing the three things that normally stop someone from trying something new: cost, handled by the discount, planning, handled by same-day booking instead of committing weeks out, and decision fatigue, handled by a curated, time-boxed feed instead of an open-ended search. It’s a small mechanic, but it maps directly onto the parallel-lives prompt. It turns the pottery class you keep meaning to try from a someday-thing into a tonight-thing.

Adlib placed 2nd out of the teams competing at Converge 2026. The judges’ feedback kept coming back to one thing: the UX, the business model, and the pitch story all pointed at the same idea, giving the concept a clear answer for why both sides of the marketplace, businesses with unsold capacity and people looking for a low-stakes way in, would actually use it.

Felicia Wang, George Gu, and Eva Chong were absolutley wonderful to work with. A five-hour deck doesn’t come together without everyone pulling in the same direction. Thanks also to FLUX for organizing Converge and to the judges for a thoughtful, fast-moving event.
